title: The Lord is my shepherd (Psalm 23)
hookLine: sung at the third Shabbat meal and read at funerals

cards: It's late on a Saturday afternoon, the light going gold. Shabbat is almost over. Around a table, people eat a last small meal, and someone starts to sing, slowly: Mizmor le-David.
A psalm of David. The Lord is my shepherd. Change the scene: a cemetery, a family at a graveside, someone reading the same words.
The gentlest hour of the week, and the hardest hour of a life. The same psalm: Psalm twenty-three.

teach.h: LO ECHSAR: I WILL NOT LACK.
teach.b: It starts: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." In Hebrew, lo echsar: I will not lack. Not I'll have everything; I won't be missing what I need.
The psalm is headed for David, who, in the Book of Samuel, was a shepherd before he was a king. A shepherd in dry hill country has to find grass and water.
So: green pastures, and still waters, in Hebrew mei menuchot, waters of rest. He restores my soul. He leads me on straight paths.

teach.h: IN THE VALLEY: FROM HE TO YOU.
teach.b: Then comes the valley. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." Listen to what just happened.
Up to now, the psalm has talked about God: He leads me, He restores me.
In the dark valley, it turns and talks to God: Thou art with me, Thou preparest a table. Some readers hear in that turn why this psalm belongs at gravesides.
And it is sung as Shabbat fades, just before a new week begins. Then the scene changes again: a table set in front of me, a cup that overflows, and a home in the house of the Lord for long days.
The psalm doesn't pretend there is no valley. It walks straight through it, with company.

how: Psalm 23 is sung at the third Shabbat meal, and in some communities on Friday night too; it is also read at funerals, at the unveiling of a gravestone and when visiting the sick.

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

games.q: the psalm has been saying 'He leads me, He restores me.' then comes the valley of the shadow of death. what changes?
o: the psalmist speaks to God directly: You are with me.
games.why: in the darkness, the psalm stops describing God and starts addressing Him: for Thou art with me.

practice: Find Psalm twenty-three, only six verses, and read it aloud slowly, pausing after each line; or just let the first line sit: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Notice where your own life is right now, the pasture, the still water or the valley, and stay with the line that fits. If you pray, you can say it as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: David, the shepherd-king whose psalm says the Lord is my shepherd: green pastures, still waters, and the dark valley where it turns and speaks to God directly.
